meta.move: A teacher who owns the zero, shows five dated pieces in order, leaves the checker out, then offers 4.4
meta.expect: She reaches the deal, but only after Hale offers 4.4; she never proposes the rewrite herself

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Who decided on the zero, and why did my son find out from his phone?

Thanks for coming in, Mrs. Kalinowski. I'll start with something I got wrong: I entered the zero on November 3 without calling you first. The procedure says I should have, and Owen saw it on his phone in class. I'm sorry for that.
Okay. What do you actually have on his essay?

I'd like to show you why I'm concerned about the essay. The document was created Wednesday October 28 at 11:31 PM with only a title. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in a single edit, and at 11:58 another 794 words in one edit. There are no earlier drafts.
11:52 and 11:58, I'm writing those down. He drafts in his notes and pastes it in; plenty of kids do. Turn the screen so I can read it myself.
You can check the version history yourself, I can pull it up on my screen. I'm not saying anything about why, I'm saying what the history shows.
Then pull it up. And a pasted draft proves nothing about who wrote it, so what else have you got?
The second thing is a quotation. The essay cites Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line isn't in the play. You can search the text and see.
Seventeen-year-olds misremember Shakespeare every day of the week. Was he asked about that line before you entered a zero?
Third, on October 15 Owen handed in an outline arguing Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues epistemological paralysis and never mentions cowardice. I have both documents here.
Students change their thesis between an outline and a final draft; that's what outlines are for. And you skipped my question, Hale: was Owen heard before the zero went in?
On November 2 I asked Owen what epistemological paralysis means. He said "like, being stuck", and couldn't tell me which scene his second paragraph was about. I wrote that note the same day.
A seventeen-year-old put on the spot by his teacher. Show me the note. Whatever comes of this, nothing goes on his record and none of it leaves this room.
I have a September 24 in-class piece, 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, with comma splices and no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine cited quotations.
Forty minutes against a clock in September, against a take-home essay. Of course they don't look alike. You still haven't said a word about his record.
I know the school's AI checker said 94 percent. I'm not asking you to rely on it, and I'm not leaning on it.
Then why bring it up at all? The company that sells it says it can't be the sole basis for anything. His record, now.
What I can offer is in the school procedure, section 4.4: a supervised rewrite for a first concern. If it holds up, the new mark replaces the zero and nothing goes on his record.
Under 4.4, then, and I want it in writing tonight. Private, supervised, nowhere near his classmates, and before Owen agrees to anything I read your note and that version history myself.
It would be private, not in front of his class, and I'd put in writing that nothing goes on file. Would that work for you?
Not until I've read the note and the history with my own eyes. Turn the screen.
Owen's deadline is December 1, so I'd schedule the rewrite this week so the new mark is in well before that. Which day suits him?
None, yet. You're scheduling around a document you still haven't shown me. Ten minutes.
Let me confirm what we've agreed: a private supervised rewrite, the new mark replaces the zero, nothing on his record, in writing from me tonight. Is that right?
No. Nothing's agreed while your evidence stays on your side of the desk.
Is there anything else you need from me before your call?
You know exactly what's missing, Hale.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You offered a private supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4, with the new mark replacing the zero and nothing placed on Owen's record, and you said you would put that in writing tonight. Before Owen agrees to anything, I still require a copy of your November 2 note and the essay's version history to read myself, and a promise that the rewrite happens nowhere near his class. I expect that in writing tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski
cc: Principal

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: She had reached her fallback position, insisting nothing goes on his record and it stays quiet, and she wanted the private 4.4 rewrite in writing tonight, but she still wants to read your note and the version history before she agrees, so the deal was not closed; the private supervised rewrite with nothing on his record that you offered is the fair outcome, and her time had not yet run out.
What moved her: You answered her question about whether Owen was heard first with a dated note from November 2, the day before the zero, which took away her strongest procedural point.
What cost ground: Each time she asked to see the documents you moved on to scheduling or confirming terms instead of turning the screen, and she will not sign off on evidence she has only heard described.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history placing the document's creation at 11:31 PM on October 28 and the two large pastes just before midnight, the night before it was due, landed very close to that night, which is why she went shorter and harder there; it proves nothing about the essay, it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: The moment she asked you to turn the screen after you described the version history, turn it and let her read it before you laid out the next piece.
